title: Sonnets from the Portuguese
short: The sequence was written during EBB's courtship by Robert Browning (1845-46) and published in Poems (1850); this is the penultimate sonnet.
body: Elizabeth Barrett wrote the sonnets privately during the courtship that ended in her secret marriage to Robert Browning in September 1846; she showed them to him only in 1849. They were published in the second edition of her Poems (1850), and the title presented them as if translated, disguising their autobiographical content; it alludes to Robert's pet name for her, linked with her poem 'Catarina to Camoens'. A supposed private edition dated Reading 1847 was a forgery by Thomas J. Wise, exposed by Carter and Pollard in 1934. This is the forty-third of the forty-four sonnets in the sequence.

title: Let me count the ways
short: The poem answers its question by enumeration: the anaphora 'I love thee' recurs nine times, as in a litany.
body: Counting the ways of love is a rhetorical figure with roots in the catalogue or blazon of Renaissance love poetry, but here the speaker enumerates not the beloved's beauties but the dimensions of her own love. The repeated 'I love thee', in the manner of a liturgical litany, gives the sonnet its incantatory force. Critics have observed that the poem's fame has made it seem conventional, whereas in its context it is unusual: a woman speaking as the active lover in a genre where women were traditionally silent objects of praise (Mermin).

title: Petrarchan sonnet
short: An Italian (Petrarchan) sonnet: octave abbaabba, sestet cdcdcd, but the sense runs through without the usual sharp turn at line 9.
body: The rhymes are ways/height/sight/Grace/everyday's/candlelight/Right/Praise (abbaabba) and use/faith/lose/breath/choose/death (cdcdcd). EBB favoured the stricter Italian form, which she used throughout the sequence, and treated it freely: enjambment carries the octave's syntax across line-ends ('height / My soul can reach'), and the volta at line 9 is softened, as the catalogue continues. The real turn comes in the final line, which moves from life to 'after death'.

title: depth and breadth and height
short: Echoes St Paul's prayer that believers may comprehend 'the breadth, and length, and depth, and height' of the love of Christ.
body: In Ephesians 3:18-19 Paul prays that the Ephesians 'may be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge'. The echo frames human love in terms of divine love and its measureless dimensions. The spatial terms also give the love a quasi-physical extent, reaching as far as the soul can stretch 'when feeling out of sight' (groping beyond what is visible) towards the limits of existence.

title: the ends of Being and ideal Grace
short: The furthest limits and purposes of existence and the perfection of divine favour; 'ends' means both boundaries and goals.
body: 'Ends' can mean the outer limits of being, which the soul gropes towards 'out of sight', or its final purposes (the philosophical sense of 'end' as telos). 'Ideal Grace' may be divine grace in its perfect form or ideal beauty, so the phrase combines theology and aesthetics. EBB, a learned reader of Greek and of Christian Platonism, compresses metaphysical ambition into an abstract line; some readers find it the poem's most strained moment, others its most daring claim that love reaches toward the absolute.

title: everyday's / Most quiet need
short: After the cosmic dimensions, love is measured at the level of ordinary daily needs, by day and by night.
body: The sonnet moves from the infinite to the domestic: the love meets the plainest needs of every day, 'by sun and candlelight', that is, day and evening. The contrast between the metaphysical and the homely is a feature of the whole sequence, which draws on the circumstances of EBB's invalid life in her Wimpole Street room. Leighton and Mermin note how the sonnets give equal weight to everyday intimacy and spiritual exaltation.

sources.cite: Angela Leighton, Elizabeth Barrett Browning (Harvester, 1986)

title: freely, as men strive for Right
short: She loves without compulsion, as people freely choose to struggle for justice; the capitalised 'Right' suggests a moral and political ideal.
body: The comparison links private love to public virtue. EBB was deeply engaged with political causes (later the Italian Risorgimento and the anti-slavery cause), and 'Right' here suggests justice pursued voluntarily, without reward. 'Freely' also recalls the theology of grace freely given. The paired line (l. 8) gives a matching moral analogy, so that ll. 7-8 form a balanced pair within the octave.

sources.cite: Sandra Donaldson et al., eds., The Works of Elizabeth Barrett Browning, 5 vols (Pickering & Chatto, 2010), notes to Sonnets from the Portuguese

title: purely, as they turn from Praise
short: Her love is pure as the humility of those who decline praise: it seeks no reward or recognition.
body: To 'turn from Praise' is to refuse flattery or the desire for fame, an act of moral purity. EBB, at the time of the courtship the better-known poet of the two, was acutely conscious of reputation; the line implies a love free of self-regard. The capitalised abstractions (Being, Grace, Right, Praise) give the octave a quasi-allegorical dignity, and the parallel syntax of ll. 7-8 ('freely, as ... purely, as ...') shows the poem's controlled, almost liturgical balance before the more personal sestet.

title: the passion put to use / In my old griefs
short: The intensity she once spent on suffering is now redirected into love; 'passion' keeps its old sense of suffering as well as its new sense of ardour.
body: 'Passion' originally meant suffering (as in Christ's Passion). EBB had endured long illness and grief, including her mother's death in 1828 and the drowning of her favourite brother Edward ('Bro') at Torquay in 1840, which she blamed on herself. The line suggests that emotional energy formerly consumed by sorrow is now 'put to use' in love. The sestet thus turns to her personal history, as the octave dealt in abstractions.

title: my childhood's faith
short: She loves with the whole-hearted trust of a child's belief, before experience brought doubt.
body: The phrase suggests unquestioning trust, as in Christ's saying that the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who become 'as little children' (Matthew 18:3). Coupled with 'old griefs', it spans her whole life, from early belief to later sorrow, and prepares for the next lines on a love she 'seemed to lose' with her 'lost saints'. The suggestion is that the new love recovers a capacity for unreserved belief that grief and illness had eroded, a movement of restoration traced across the whole sequence.

sources.cite: Matthew 18:3 (KJV)

title: my lost saints
short: Either the beloved dead (her mother and brother) or the idealised figures of childhood faith whom she ceased to venerate; editors offer both readings.
body: 'Saints' may refer to people she revered who have died, chiefly her mother and her brother Edward, so that the love 'lost' with them is the love she gave her family. Alternatively it may mean the saints and religious ideals of her early faith, a fervour she lost as she grew up. Both readings imply that this new love restores an earlier capacity for devotion. The dash and the sudden exclamation that follow ('I love thee with the breath, / Smiles, tears, of all my life!') break the measured catalogue with overflowing feeling.

title: if God choose ... after death
short: The sonnet ends by projecting love beyond the grave, conditional on God's will: love perfected in eternity.
body: 'If God choose' places the claim under providence, a humility that tempers the boast. 'But' means 'only': death will only increase her love. The idea of love surviving death is an old topos of love poetry, but here it also reflects EBB's earnest Christian hope of reunion. Given her chronic illness and expectation of early death, the line had personal weight. It turns the catalogue of the present into a promise for eternity.
